layout_details.content: # INTRODUCTION
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The use of product data is an essential part of electronic business. Product selection, business transactions, maintenance procedures, etc., rely on the availability of data about products and services. To ensure a common understanding and a general treatment of product data, classification and dictionary systems are used to define their essential technical parameters or to categorize products.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The standards of the series IEC 61360 specify rules for structure and content of collections of product properties and its classification structures. In most cases the classes and properties contained in such collections are intuitively understandable. But, unfortunately, creating the information objects and their textual content, such as definitions, has proved to be a demanding task with potential pitfalls and problems. For avoiding such difficulties explanatory material and sections of other standards are collected in this part of IEC 61360 providing the necessary knowledge for successfully creating classes and properties. Thus, IEC 61360-6 provides guidance for specifying the information content of IEC 61360 classes and properties.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: This part of IEC 61360 is intended for domain specialists who are technical experts in their specific technical domain. The domain specialists do not necessarily have an in-depth knowledge of IEC 61360-1 or IEC 61360-2.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 1 Scope
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: This part of IEC 61360 provides guidance for the definition of concepts that are used to describe classes and properties submitted for update of the content of IEC Common Data Dictionary (IEC CDD). This includes
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - a basic understanding of key concepts and procedures used within IEC CDD;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - a binding reference for quality control of IEC 61360 compliant dictionary content;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - guidance on documents where necessary in-depth knowledge can be acquired (see Clause 2 and Annex D).
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - This part of IEC 61360 includes the following subjects:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - basic overview about fundamental concepts of IEC 61360;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - formulating definitions and other textual elements;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - overview of IEC maintenance procedure for IEC CDD;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - checklist for providing input to the IEC CDD content.

layout_details.content: ## 4 Data structure fundamentals
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 4.1 General
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: For the convenience of the reader, Clause 4 describes key concepts used in the IEC 61360 series and in related standards in a generic form for creating a basic understanding of the information objects that make up IEC 61360 compliant dictionaries. For the detailed, normative information, please refer to Part 1 and Part 2 of IEC 61360. Additional information can be found in $ [ 7 ]^{1} $ and [8].
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: An IEC 61360 compliant dictionary provides an ordered collection of concepts and characteristics that can be used for describing products or services in data sheets, engineering tools, or electronic business applications, etc. These items may be any material or non-material products, services, functions, locations, documentations, etc. All concepts and characteristics shall be valid within a well defined domain and shall always have a definition.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: For this the understanding of the following fundamental concepts is essential:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - class;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - property;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - attribute.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 4.2 Class
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: A class is an abstraction of a set of products.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE 1 IEC 61360-2 differentiates between various kinds of classes. For the purpose of this part "class" is understood as "categorization class" (see 3.1.3, NOTE 5).
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: These products all serve the same purpose or fulfil the same function and share a number of common peculiarities.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Thus, classes serve multiple purposes
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - establishing a classification system that allows easy sorting of an item into this system of concepts and thus specifying the nature of the item in question;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE The taxonomy of species, introduced by Carl von Linné at 1735, is an early representative of a classification system. His groupings for animals remain to this day even though the groupings themselves have been significantly changed since their conception.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - providing scoping information for the assigned characteristics and thus providing information about their intended domains of uses;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - grouping of characteristics into easily manageable sets.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: A class may be seen as a placeholder for all products of the same kind, such as the class of amplifiers. A product is any material or non-material object being defined for some purpose. Material products include concepts such as articles, goods, material commodities, etc., whereas non-material products include concepts such as services or consulting activities.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The creation of a consistent classification system that properly reflects a business domain can be quite difficult. Such classification systems should be consistent, comprehensive, and concise.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE 2 An object that complies with the abstraction defined by a class is called a class member.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE Figure 1 shows a classification tree for amplifiers.

Such a class can be split further down into subclasses like operational amplifiers and ac-coupled amplifiers as shown in Figure 1.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 4.3 Property
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Properties specify the characteristics of the members of classes. Each property specifies one characteristic and the set of associated properties fully specifies all characteristics of the members of that class. All members of a class share the same set of properties.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: In many cases properties have a unit of measure, and in some cases they have an assigned value list or are constrained by conditions.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE Properties express characteristics such as length, diameter, or rated voltage.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Additionally, each property shall be defined in a class. This class specifies the domain of application of the property and the property shall be meaningful for the domain specified by this class and its subclasses.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 4.5 Key attributes of IEC CDD entries
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 4.5.1 Overview
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Key elements of IEC CDD entries are the attributes that assign meaning to properties and classes. The most important attributes are:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - definition;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - note;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: remark.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Textual information kept in the attributes of the objects such as preferred name, definition, or note, are the backbone of the information content of the dictionary. Thus, great care shall be applied to create syntactically and semantically error-free texts.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The quality of an IEC CDD entry mainly depends on the information given within these attributes. Thus, it is important to draft their content carefully.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 4.5.2 Definition
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Attribute name: definition
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Attribute definition:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: statement that describes the meaning of a property in an unambiguous and unique manner to permit its differentiation from all other properties
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 1 Definition of "arcing distance":
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## arcing distance
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: value of the shortest distance in air external to the insulator between metallic parts normally having the operating voltage between them.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Comments: Conventions and requirements:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: a) Any definition shall be derived from the original definition as appearing in the latest corresponding IEC or ISO standards, if available.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: b) Where possible, definitions of properties shall be independent from specific classes. Thus, reuse of the properties in other classes is supported.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: c) ISO 704 should be used as a basis for the writing of the definition.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: d) The unit of measure shall not be included in the definition.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: e) The level information should not be included in the definition.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE Level information can be specified in attribute Level type.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: f) The semantic context(s) should be included in the definition, if this is essential for the understanding of its meaning.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: g) If the concept requires a limitation of its applicability this shall be explicitly expressed in the definition.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 2 There exist different semantics of the term "rated voltage"; within products $ \geq1 $ kV, the terms rated voltage express the maximum voltage for which a product is being designed and can be operated. This is currently not applicable to products less than 1kV.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: h) If dependency relations are an inherent part of the concept, these shall be included in the definition.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 3 Definition of the quantitative property "reverse recovery time":
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## reverse recovery time
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: value of the time required for the reverse current of a diode to recover to a specified value, when switched from a specified forward current to a specified reverse voltage, at specified conditions
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: i) In the case conditions are specified, the definition should end with the wording "at specified condition(s)".
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: j) If the concept represents a kind of average value, the method of calculating the average shall be designated, by using a term that designates the method, such as "arithmetic mean", "geometric mean", "median", or "mode", either in the preferred name or in the definition.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Obligation: mandatory
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content:
Attribute name: note

Attribute definition: statement which provides further information on the definition which is essential to the understanding of that definition
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Comments: EXAMPLE The property "reverse recovery time" is further clarified by a note: "The reverse recovery time is measured as the time interval between $ t_{0} $ , the point where the forward current crosses the zero current axis, and the instant when for decreasing values of $ i_{R} $ a line through the points for 0,9 $ I_{RM} $ and 0,25 $ I_{RM} $ crosses the zero current axis."
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Obligation: optional
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 4.5.4 Remark
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content:
Attribute name: remark

Attribute definition: additional information in text for understanding the meaning of the definition
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content:
Comments: the remark shall not change the meaning of the definition

Obligation: optional
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 5 Writing of definitional content
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 5.1 Basic requirements
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: A definition shall define a concept as a unit with a unique intension or extension. For additional detail on terminological principles see Annex E, ISO 704:2009, or ISO/IEC Directives, Part 2:2016, Clause 16.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The following basic requirements apply for definitions:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - Definitions shall be provided in the singular form;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## EXAMPLE
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## Lead pencil
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: pencil whose graphite core is fixed in a wooden casing that is removed for usage by sharpening
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - The content of the IEC 61360-1 attribute "preferred name" shall consequently be singular, too;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - Definitions should consist ideally of a single string of words ("sentence") that may be used to substitute the term in its original environment;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - Definitions shall start with a lowercase letter and end without a full stop.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE The quality of a dictionary is decisively influenced by the quality of its definitions.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 5.2 Principles for definition writing
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Each definition shall comprise a statement explaining what the concept or characteristic is. The statement is made up of a subject, copula and predicate. The subject is the designation, the copula is understood to be the verb "is" and the predicate constitutes the definition.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## EXAMPLE 1
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## lead pencil
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: pencil whose graphite core is fixed in a wooden casing that is removed for usage by sharpening
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Note 1 to entry To be used for writing or making marks, a lead pencil must be sharpened at least at one end.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The entry should read as follows: " [A] lead pencil [is a] pencil whose graphite core is fixed in a wooden casing that is removed for usage by sharpening".
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The words making up the definition should be common language as specified by the reference works for English language recommended by the IEC Directives (see ISO/IEC Directives, Part 2:2016, 8.5) and should not need further explanation.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE A concept or characteristic has always a definition regardless if its designation, i.e. preferred name (see IEC 61360-1), is taken from commonly used dictionaries or other common sources.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 2 The word "computer" used in the body of a definition does not need further explanation if its intended meaning is in accordance to common language as specified, e.g., in The Concise Oxford Dictionary (see ISO/IEC Directives, Part 2:2016, 8.2) whereas a concept or characteristic designated as "computer" always requires a definition.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: If expert language is unavoidable or misunderstandings are likely the definition should be complemented by a reference to acknowledged sources such as International Standards or expert literature where further explanation can be found.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 5.3 Conciseness
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Ideally, definitions shall be as simple and concise as possible. Complex definitions can contain several dependent clauses, but carefully written definitions contain only that information which makes the concept unique. On the other hand, no information required for achieving the uniqueness of the concept or characteristic shall be hidden. All information essential for defining the concept shall be disclosed.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 1 The phrase "... and considering other conditions" in a definition states the necessity of additional information for the definition without providing this information and, thus, violates the above requirement.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Any additional descriptive information deemed necessary should be included in a note.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## EXAMPLE 2
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: lead pencil
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: pencil whose graphite core is fixed in a wooden casing that is removed for usage by sharpening
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Note 1 to entry To be used for writing or making marks, a lead pencil must be sharpened at least at one end.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: A definition shall describe only one concept or characteristic. It shall not include hidden definitions for any concepts used to identify qualities. Any quality that requires an explanation shall be defined separately as a concept or given in a note.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## EXAMPLE 3
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 3 lead pencil pencil whose wooden casing is fixed around graphite, a soft, black form of carbon
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: This definition of "lead pencil" includes a hidden definition for the concept "graphite". The quality "a soft, black form of carbon" should be removed and used in a separate definition for the concept "graphite".
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 5.4 Principle of substitution
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The substitution principle shall be used to test the validity of a definition. A definition is valid if it can replace a designation in a text without loss of or change in meaning.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 5.5 Deficient definitions
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 5.5.1 General
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Common types of deficient definitions are: circular, incomplete or negative definitions.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 5.5.2 Circular definitions
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: If one concept is defined using a second concept, and that second concept is defined using the term or elements of the term designating the first concept, the resulting definitions are said to be circular. Circular definitions do not add understanding of the concept and shall be avoided.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Definitions can be circular:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - within a single definition;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - within a system of definitions.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Circularity within a definition occurs when the designation is repeated to introduce the definition or an element of the designation is used as a characteristic. When formulating a definition, it is not permissible to repeat the designation to introduce the definition (see EXAMPLE 1).
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## EXAMPLE 1
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: tree height: circular definition: tree height measured from the ground surface to the top of a tree corrected definition: distance between the ground surface and the top of a tree
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The use of an element of the designation, other than the head word, as a characteristic in the definition should be avoided as much as possible (see EXAMPLE 2). However, cases exist where the name of the superordinate concept is part of the designation of the term. This part of the designation may be reused in the definition of the term.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content:
evergreen tree:

circular definition: tree with evergreen foliage

corrected definition: tree that retains its foliage throughout its lifetime
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Note, that in this example "tree" is the superordinate concept for "evergreen tree" and thus is reused in the definition of "evergreen tree".
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: In cases when the designation of the concept is very close to the name of the superordinate concept effort should be invested in finding another name for the concept to avoid misunderstandings. Even though formally correct, the definition below may easily create misunderstandings (EXAMPLE 3).
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 3 International Standard international standard published by IEC,ISO,ISO/IEC,or by ITU
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Note, that "International Standard" and "international standard" are very close and can easily be confused.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: A definition is circular within a system of definitions when two or more concepts are defined by means of each other.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 5.5.3 Incomplete definitions
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: A definition shall describe the content of the concept precisely. It shall be neither too narrow nor too broad.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Otherwise, the definition is considered incomplete. Non-essential or irrelevant characteristics in the definition can unintentionally include or exclude objects from the extension of the concept.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: A definition is considered too broad if the characteristics selected to describe the concept do not allow for objects that are implied by the definition, as part of its extension. A definition is considered too narrow if the characteristics (selected to describe the concept) allow for objects that are not implied by the definition, as part of its extension.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 1 mechanical pencil too broad: writing instrument composed of a barrel and a refill
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: By not specifying precisely the type of refills, this definition broadens the extension to include ball-point, roller-ball and felt-tip pens as well as mechanical pencils.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: too narrow: writing instrument composed of a barrel, a lead refill and push-button advance mechanism
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: By specifying a push-button advance mechanism, this definition narrows the extension to exclude those mechanical pencils using other types of advance mechanisms.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: corrected definition: writing instrument composed of a barrel, a lead refill and a lead-advance mechanism
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: In adapting an existing definition to a specific subject field or context, care should be taken not to change the extension of the concept. A change to the extension leads to a new unit and a different concept. Similarly, changes to any of the essential characteristics in a definition result in a new concept.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: A particular context rarely refers to all the objects making up the extension of a concept. Definitions in laws and regulations tend to be interpretive rather than defining. Definitions in International Standards should be defining rather than interpretive. If a concept is restricted to a particular interpretation for a given text, it shall be explained in the body of the International Standard rather than by creating a new concept with a narrower extension. If specification information is associated with the concept, then this should be given in an appropriate specification clause rather than in a definition.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 2 too narrow: organization for the purposes of this regulation, bodies not operating for profit
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: This definition of "organization" does not define the concept "organization" but merely signals how to interpret the concept in a given context. From all the objects that make up extension of the concept "organization", this context considers only those not operating for profit.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 5.5.4 Negative definitions
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: A definition shall describe what a concept is, not what it is not.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content:
EXAMPLE 1

deciduous tree

inappropriate negative definition: tree other than an evergreen tree
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: deciduous tree corrected definition: tree that loses its foliage seasonally
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: However, when the absence or non-existence of a characteristic is essential to the understanding of a concept, a negative definition may be required.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 2 nonconformity: non-fulfilment of a specified requirement
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 5.6 Notes and examples
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Definitions may be complemented by one or more notes or examples. Notes and examples shall only be used for giving additional information intended to assist the understanding or use of the definition.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: They shall not contain requirements or any information considered indispensable for the use of the definition.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: When several notes occur within the same definition, they shall be designated "NOTE 1", "NOTE 2", "NOTE 3", etc. When several examples occur within the same definition, they shall be designated "EXAMPLE 1", "EXAMPLE 2", "EXAMPLE 3", etc.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: # 6 Recommendations for textual information in dictionaries according to IEC 61360 series
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.1 General
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The requirements of the ISO/IEC Directives, Part 2 [3] apply for the textual parts of IEC CDD. For the convenience of the readers, 6.2 to 6.10 below focus on the most commonly encountered problems and summarize requirements set forth in [3] or explain problems specific to dictionary entries.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.2 Recommendations that emerge from the implementation of IEC CDD
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Due to the import capabilities of the implementation of IEC CDD, certain recommendations apply.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE See also IEC 62656-1 for a detailed specification of the IEC CDD data interface.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: a) Blank fields (fields containing no data) shall be entirely empty, containing no null characters or spaces.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: b) Fields shall not contain any leading or trailing null characters or spaces.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: c) Dates shall be given in the form "yyyy-mm-dd".
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: d) Field values that extend over more than one line (notably definition, note and remark) should be typed as continuous text with no line breaks. To indicate a line break in the text, the vertical bar character ("|") shall be used.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: e) Special characters and formats such as superscript, subscript or italics, are usually lost when being transferred from one application to another. Because there is no guarantee that a target system will read them correctly, an ASCII representation is used for symbols and units in the database. For Greek letters, the SGML form is used, e.g. " α", whilst for subscripts and superscripts the control characters " _ " or " ** " should be used to start the subscript or superscript, followed by a closing curly bracket " } " after the subscript or superscript. Thus, a symbol name can appear as " α ; 1 " , to be presented as $ \alpha_{1} $ and a unit as $ \mathrm{A / m^{**}2} $ , to be presented as $ \mathrm{A / m^{2}} $ .
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.3 Languages
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The language for the reference version of all textual parts of IEC CDD shall be British English. All other languages, including the French language version, shall be derived from this reference version.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.4 Acceptable wording
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.4.1 General
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: This 6.4 gives details on the wording to be used explaining requirements or recommendations.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.4.2 Using "shall" and "shall not"
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The verbal forms "shall" and "shall not" indicate requirements to be followed to conform to the standard and from which no deviation is permitted. The words "shall" and "shall not" shall be used in normative text and shall not be used in the introduction, foreword, notes, or examples, which are informative text.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: "Shall" shall be used to denote the following:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - is to...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - is required to ...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - it is required that ...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - has to...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - only... is permitted;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - it is necessary ...
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - "Shall not" shall be used to denote the following:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - it is not allowed (permitted, acceptable, permissible)...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - is required to be not ...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - is required that... be not...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - is not to be ...
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Do not use "must" except to describe "unavoidable" situations. Do not use "may not" instead of "shall not" to express a prohibition.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.4.3 Using "must" and "must not"
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The words "must" and "must not" shall be used only to convey constraints or obligations defined outside of the document.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.4.4 Using "should" and "should not"
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The words "should" and "should not" shall be used to recommend a particularly suitable possibility or course of action without excluding others. "Should" shall be used to denote the following:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - it is recommended that ...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - ought to ...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - "Should not" shall be used to denote the following:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - it is recommended that... not;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ought not to ...
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.4.5 Use of "may" and "need not"
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The words "may" and "need not" indicate a course of action that is permissible within the limits of the standard. "May" shall be used to denote the following:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - ... is permitted;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - ... is allowed;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - ... is permissible.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - "Need not" shall be used to denote the following:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - it is not required that ...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - no ...is required.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Do not use "can" instead of "may" in this context. Do not use "possible" or "impossible" in this context.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE "May" refers to something that is permitted whereas "can" refers to something that is possible.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.4.6 Use of "can" and "cannot"
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The words "can" and "cannot" indicate possibility and capability.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: "Can" shall be used to denote the following:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - to be able to ...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - to be in a position to ...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - there is a possibility of ...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - it is possible to ...
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - "Cannot" shall be used to denote the following:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - to be unable to ...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - to be not in a position to ...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - there is no possibility of ...;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - it is impossible to ...
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE "Can" refers to something that is possible whereas "may" refers to something that is permitted.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.4.7 Use of "i.e.", "e.g.", and "etc."
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Do not use "i.e." and "e.g.". Instead, use "that is" and "for example". If using "that is," the list that follows shall be all inclusive whereas "for example," shall only list some of the possibilities and shall only appear in a note or example. Likewise, do not use "etc.". End the series prior to the "etc." being certain to use a serial comma before the "and" (added if not already there). To state that the series is incomplete, use "such as" at the start of the series.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.4.8 Use of abbreviations
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Use of abbreviations should be avoided. A list of abbreviations is not mandatory for IEC 61360 dictionaries. Thus, no unambiguous interpretation of an abbreviation can be ensured. If an abbreviation has to be used the unabridged form shall be included in brackets when the abbreviation is used.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE The abbreviation "AC" can stand for several meanings such as "alternating current", "air condition", "Acetyl", and "Actinium".
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.5 Quotations from standards or documented sources
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: In many cases it is desirable to introduce concepts from other sources such as standards or acknowledged expert literature into the dictionary. International, national or industry standards may be referenced; however, if there is also an ISO or IEC standard, the ISO or IEC standard shall be used.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Before a term and a definition are established for a concept, it should be ascertained that no other term and definition for that concept exist in another document. In ISO, refer to the concept database: <http://cdb.iso.org>. In the case of electrotechnical terms, refer to the International Electrotechnical Vocabulary (IEC 60050): <http://www.electropedia.org>.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Information objects such as classes or properties shall be referenced by giving their International Registration Data Identifier (IRDI).
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE See IEC 61360-1 and ISO/IEC 11179-6 for additional information on identification of information objects using IRDI.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 1 Example of a reference using the International Registration Data Identifier: "[SOURCE: 0112/2//61360_4#AAF307]"
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: References to a particular element of another standard shall include the clause referred to as well as the reference number of the standard and the year of publication. ISO or IEC Technical Specifications, Publicly Available Specifications, and Technical Reports may be referenced in the same way.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 2 [SOURCE: ISO/IEC Directives, Part 2:2016, 16.5.9]
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 3 [SOURCE: ISO 80000-1:2009, 3.3, modified - Note 3 has been deleted.]
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: In addition, any publicly available document, such as expert literature, having wide acceptance and authoritative status as well as being publicly available may be referenced.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Any reference to literature containing explanatory information about the definition should go into a note. Especially if referring to documents other than standards the wording of the text may be not in line with the ISO/ IEC rules for definitions. Minor formal adaptations of the text such as omitting the definite article at the beginning of a definition and leaving out the punctuation at the end need not be indicated as modification.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: More extensive modifications shall be indicated as paraphrase. When paraphrasing of the original definition cannot be avoided, great care shall be taken not to modify the original meaning.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: References to a particular element of a document other than a standard shall include the name of the author, the year of publication and the number of the page where the source text occurs (see EXAMPLE 4). The full reference shall be contained in the attribute "Source document of definition" (see EXAMPLE 5).
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 4 [SOURCE: IUPAC (1997, p.347), modified - paraphrased content]
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 5 IUPAC: Compendium of Chemical Terminology, $ 2^{\mathrm{nd}} $ ed. compiled by A. D. McNaught and A. Wilkinson. Oxford: Blackwell Scientific Publications, 1997
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Summaries are not a valid citation of a source document.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.6 Use of quotation marks
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Quotation marks shall be used to set off words or phrases that may confuse the reader if not marked. Double quotation marks "..." denote quoted text or particular text string values.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.7 Spelling
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The spelling of the names of organizations, and their abbreviations, shall be as used by those organizations, in English or French.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: To facilitate understanding by all readers, the style shall be as simple and concise as possible. This is particularly important for those readers whose mother tongue is not one of the official languages of ISO and IEC.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The following reference works for language are recommended (see ISO/IEC Directives, Part 2:2016, 8.2):
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - for English: The Shorter Oxford English Dictionary, The Concise Oxford Dictionary, The Collins Concise English Dictionary, Webster's New World College Dictionary or Chambers Concise Dictionary;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - for French: Dictionnaire Le Robert, Dictionnaire Larousse and Dictionnaire des difficultés de la langue française, V. Thomas, Larousse.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Abbreviated terms shall be used with care, and their use shall be limited to those cases where it is not likely to cause confusion (see ISO/IEC Directives, Part 2:2016, 8.3).
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE Spelling checkers associated with word processor programs rarely, even in the "British spelling" mode, conform to the required dictionary.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Note the correct spelling of the following:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - numbers from one to nine shall be spelled out in words;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - modelling, modelled, centre, colour, coordinate, faceted, litre, metre, millimetre, neighbour, organization;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: and the preferred spelling of the following:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: instantiation.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: If American English is unavoidable, e.g. for specialist terms, the postfix "en US-" shall be added after the passage in question.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Other languages such as French, German, Japanese, etc. may be created under the responsibility of the respective National Committee.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Localized versions of dictionary objects should carry their own version and/or revision identifiers due to possible latencies or error corrections during the translation process.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.8 Hyphenation
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: In general, hyphenation should be used to improve readability and appearance. Hyphenation shall follow the rules given in the reference works for language as specified in 6.7. These special terms shall be hyphenated as follows:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - non-zero;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - two-dimensional, three-dimensional (may be abbreviated as "2D" or "3D");
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - X-axis, Y-axis, and Z-axis.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Abbreviations shall not be divided by a line break.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.9 Words to avoid
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Avoid the use of words that are corporate trademarks. If the use of trademarks is necessary, accompany the word by the trademark symbol " $ ^{\mathrm{T M}} $ " or the registered trademark symbol $ ^{ \textcircled{R}} $ as appropriate.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE The title of ISO TS 10303-27 is "Implementation methods: Java $ ^{\mathrm{TM}} $ programming language binding to the standard data access interface with Internet/Intranet extensions". Since the word "Java" in this context is a trademark, it is accompanied by the symbol $ ^{\mathrm{TM}} $ .
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Avoid the following words to provide editorial consistency:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - "and/or": rather than use this form, expand the explanation and present both cases;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - "datums": the plural of "datum" is "data". If one is tempted to use "datums", change it to "datum points" or "datum lines" or "datum planes" as the case may be;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - "utilise": use "use" instead;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - "in other words": this phrase is often used to join two alternative definitions of a term or concept: the alternative definitions should be reviewed and reconciled.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: However, if a project cites another ISO or IEC standard, or broadly accepted terminology for a given domain for a specific meaning of a prohibited term, the editor should follow the cited spelling.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 6.10 Frequently used words
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The following terms are used frequently in standards. To ensure editorial consistency, they should be used only in precisely defined contexts.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - between/among: use "between" to mean "exactly two"; use "among" to mean "two or more than two";
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - data: "data" is a plural noun and requires a plural verb, that is, "data are" not "data is". In cases where the number of items is important a wording such as "a piece of data", "a set of data", "two sets of data" may be used;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - if: if an "if" clause ends in a comma, do not follow it with the word "then";
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - presentation: do not use "presentation" for "representation". "Presentation" should be restricted to situations with visual aspects;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - which: do not use "which" in place of "that". "That" introduces a defining phrase; "which" introduces an informational phrase.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 7 Names
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 7.1 General
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Names are used to designate objects, such as classes or properties. They play an important role as enablers of human communication about the objects and their meaning. Even though names should be unique, it is not guaranteed that names are unambiguous whereas identifiers shall be always unique.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 7.2 Preferred name
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: When a new entry is added, a preferred name has to be selected. This name should match the most commonly used English name within the industry for which the represented concept is used.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The use of the same preferred name should be avoided as much as possible within a close family of classes. In particular the same preferred name for different properties that may be potentially applied to the same class should be avoided.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: If such is inevitable, care must be taken to clearly differentiate the definitions of such properties.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE Within IEC, British English is requested.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 7.3 Synonymous name
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Alternatives to a preferred name may be used to accomplish global understanding. Within a given language, for example British English, other English terms deviating from the British- English may be used.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 7.4 Names shall not infer range values
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Entries shall not be named or defined in a way so as to infer multiple values.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Entries whose preferred names or synonymous names containing the word "range" should be examined closely for violation of this constraint.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Instances of a property definition, such as "Supply Voltage", can be reported in an interchange with a "min" and "max" data type qualifier. In this case, there should not be two different property definitions with names like "Supply Voltage Minimum" and "Supply Voltage Maximum".
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: However, the property definition "OFF-state Leakage Current" is normally reported in a datasheet only in the context of a maximum leakage, which may be positive or negative, depending on some other voltage characteristic. So the definition semantics should state something like, "...the absolute value of the maximum current leakage...", so that an interchange reports a single, positive number with clear semantics.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 7.5 Names shall not imply product packaging
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Names should be associated with unit items and not be dependent on packaging or any other aspect of the supply chain. Exceptions to this rule may be made where a unique need, an unambiguous definition, and availability of information (sourceabilty) support the rigour required to maintain a single class set.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE Weight is a valid characteristic. Weight (per gross) is not valid.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 8 Units of measure
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: A property of measurement type shall belong to one quantity at most. If a property can be defined with multiple units in different quantities, the property should be divided into an appropriate number of properties so that all the units of each property shall belong to the same quantity.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE Load regulation of logic ICs for power supply can be conceptually expressed with a unit either of $ \mu\mathrm{V} / \mathrm{mA}, $ $ \% / \mathrm{mA}, $ $ \% $ mV, or $ \Omega $ . Those units belong to different quantities, therefore, properties for those units are defined by each quantity.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: If a unit is specified for a measurement type property, it is recommended to specify it by its code defined in IEC TS 62720 which is also available online from the IEC CDD, for assured computer sensible identification of the unit.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE Maintenance work and possible extensions of the IEC TS 62720 units will take place in an IEC database. Thus, IEC TS 62720:2013 can become outdated.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Preference shall be given to SI units. If there are alternative units to be selected for a property, they should be specified. All alternative units shall belong to the same quantity.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 9 Import of data into IEC CDD
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: IEC 62656-1 specifies the logical structure and layout of the spreadsheet interface of IEC CDD. This structure allows definition, import, export or transfer of content. To maintain consistency and avoid loss of data always complete rows of an IEC 62656-1 compliant data set should be uploaded to IEC CDD during import. All fields of a row will be used to update the related fields in IEC CDD.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: IEC 61360-1 and IEC 62656-2 provide essential guidance about use and structure of IEC CDD data and are highly recommended as background material for deeper understanding.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 10 Quality of content
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The originator of new or updated content for IEC CDD shall ensure that
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - updates or corrections are always based on the latest version of IEC CDD content;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - effort has been taken to prepare correct and consistent upload data.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: As Annex C a checklist is provided that shall serve as guide for those who plan to supply input to the dictionary. The checklist addresses common problems that were identified in the past.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The application of the checklist before submission of data for IEC CDD is imperative. Additionally, the IEC CDD database interface performs checks of the data files during import.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: It is recommended that involved persons acquire knowledge on IEC 61360-1.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## 11 Contributing content and copyright issues
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Proposing and standardizing classes and properties is a process in which various parties are involved.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The following cases occur:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - Input by an authorized person or body also referred to as "proposer" (see Figure 5);
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - Content already contained in published standards (see Figure 6);
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - Database maintenance (see Figure 7).
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE 1 The overlapping areas in Figure 5 to Figure 7 indicate close cooperation between the involved groups.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: By submitting content for storage, discussion, or publication in IEC CDD the proposer implicitly declares that the submitted content may be exploited freely according to the rules stated in the license statement of IEC CDD. No economic rights (such as copyright or intellectual property rights) shall apply that restrict the above use of the submitted matter (see [1]).
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE 2 All items contained in IEC CDD are subject to the IEC/ISO copyright rules unless otherwise explicitly stated (see ISO/IEC Directives, Part 1:2016, 2.13).
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Figure 5 - Input by an authorized person or body
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Figure 6- Contributing content already contained in published standards
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## Annex A (informative)
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## Use of tools to check consistency of data
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Creating consistent and error-free data for upload to a dictionary can be difficult. The necessary versatility of the underlying data models and broad range of requirements that have to be met call for data structures having some complexity. Thus, software tools supporting the creation and checking of the relevant information objects should be used.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Parcelmaker $ ^{2} $ , a tool based on Microsoft Office Excel $ ^{3} $ , supports creating and interpreting IEC 61360-1 and IEC 61360-2 as well as ISO 13584-42 compliant data in IEC 62656-1 format. Error checking functions and functions providing an improved overview on the data greatly help to avoid inconsistencies and other imperfections of the data.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: IEC 62656-1 is a spreadsheet representation for data based on IEC 61360-1 and IEC 61360-2/ ISO 13584-42 data models. This representation was specifically designed to support users working in office environments without access to special purpose software. In addition, IEC 62656-1 is used by IEC CDD as data format for import and export.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: From IEC Collaboration space an IEC 62656-1 compliant Microsoft Office Excel template for use with Parcelmaker $ ^{ \circ} $ may be downloaded. The minimum information content of IEC 61360-1 data sets is marked with "MAND" within the spreadsheets. Registered IEC experts may find the latest version of the template at (password required):
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: http://collaboration.iec.ch/LotusQuickr/other_sc3dworkingmaterial/Main.nsf/h_Toc/0798B0A3E E8F4DF0C1257C200057721F/?OpenDocument
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: # Annex B (normative)
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: # Scope and field of application of proposed data
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: When providing technically new content to IEC CDD adequate explanatory information about the planned content shall be provided.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: This information shall consist of several slides explaining
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - scope or field of application of the proposed data;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - applicable standard documents or expert literature;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - stakeholders and
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: - point(s) of contact for the proposed change request including address and email.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The information should enable the members of the involved committees such as the Validation Team for IEC CDD, its participating National Committees or other involved Technical Committees to understand scope and use of the proposed data set.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The material shall be sufficient to allow the National Committees to identify experts for the participation in the evaluation and validation process of the proposed data.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: # Annex C (normative)
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## Checklist
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## C.1 General
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: IEC CDD is a dictionary where classes and associated properties are being collected, serving as international reference library easing the communication between business partners.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The below checklist may serve as guide for those who plan to provide input to the dictionary. It is recommended that involved persons are familiar with IEC 61360-1.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The checklist addresses common problems that were identified in the past.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## C.2 Generic issues
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Are the technical committees identified on international level within IEC which need to be involved?
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: One change request should be addressed to one technical committee only.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: For reasons of easier handling of a change request the maximum number of rows in each sheet of its documentation tables should be limited to about 100 rows. In case of large data sets the accompanying description tables may be split up into several associated sheets.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The related data set, i.e. the IEC 62656-1 conforming files, can contain more than 100 rows. This data set shall always represent the complete proposed data set.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## C.3 Extension of existing classes by adding properties
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Each of the proposed properties should be verified, whether it is independent of its class.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: If yes, provide a class where to collect all such items; if no, identify the existing class to which the new properties should belong.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 1 A property "Manufacturer" would apply to many classes as most products are being manufactured by at least one organization.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 2 A property "Vendor" will apply to many product classes as most products are being brought into the market by at least one organization.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 3 A property "Measuring principle" will apply probably only to the class dealing with measuring instruments.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The content of the attribute "Definition" should be based on valid IEC or ISO standards.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Where possible, definitions should be written in a style that they are independent of a specific class.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Reference should be made only to current IEC or ISO standards. Only in cases where IEC or ISO standards are not available, reference to publicly available National Standards or expert literature should be made.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: If requesting properties with units other than SI-units, new properties shall be specified if the property in question already exists having a SI-unit.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Units from different unit systems should not be applied to the same property. In such cases additional properties should be specified (See below).
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: In order to describe conductors with sizes in American Wire Gauge (AWG) one should specify a new property called e.g. AWG size.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Are eventually existing interdependencies considered among properties?
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 4 The rated current of a device depends on the maximum value of the temperature for which it is foreseen.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Does an attribute "symbol" exist? Is it supplied in the related attribute? Is its language independency considered? Is it correctly spelled?
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Does an attribute "short name" exist? Is it supplied in the related attribute? Is its language independency considered? Is it correctly spelled?
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Are dates always in the notion "YYYY-MM-DD"?
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The "level" construct should be applied when defining a range in quantitative properties.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE 1 To express a minimum and/or maximum value the level construct is applicable and the same property is used only once.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Was a quality check applied to the input file(s) for IEC?
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE 2 Before a work item will be accepted a formal quality check will be made by the management of the data base. If the syntax is not in line, there is a risk of the work item not being accepted due to poor quality.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: A spelling checker should be used when preparing the textual content. British English (en-UK) is the favourite language of IEC.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE 3 Within the IEC Common Data Dictionary, the English language is the leading language, and is the only one considered to be the Standard.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## C.4 Setting up new classes with associated properties
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: If the existing classes do not cover the desired concepts, a new class has to be set up with definition, preferred name, etc. The next higher class node in the hierarchy (supertype) has to be identified to which it should be related.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The classifying property has to be created which is controlling possible subclasses of the class.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: # Annex D (informative)
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## IEC Maintenance procedure for IEC standards in database format
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Annex D informs about the actual situation concerning the data base procedure as documented in ISO/IEC Directives Supplement [4].
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Annex D will not be updated if the procedure changes.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE The current version of the directives can be accessed via http://www.iec.ch/members_experts/refdocs/.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The procedure is specified in detail in ISO/IEC Directives Supplement:2016, Annex SL. Figure D.1 and Figure D.2 summarize the process.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Experience has proven that the originally specified time for resolution of evaluation issues (1 week) can be too short. Thus, a time span greater than one week for this step should be tolerated.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Figure D.1 - The normal database procedure (see ISO/IEC Directives Supplement:2016, Annex SL)

layout_details.content: # Annex E (informative)
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: # Nature of definitions and terminological principles
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: There are different ways to write definitions of concepts or terms; the two most common types of definitions are "intensional" or "extensional" definitions.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Intensional definitions indicate the superordinate concept followed by the characteristic(s) that distinguish the concept from other concepts. In practice, intensional definitions are preferable to other concept descriptions. They should be used whenever possible as they most clearly reveal the essential characteristics of a concept.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE 1 A more detailed treatise of the subject can be found in ISO 704:2009.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: NOTE 2 Intensional definitions are best used when something has a clearly-defined set of qualities, and work well for specifying sets that are too large to list in an extensional definition. It is impossible to give an extensional definition for an infinite set, but an intensional one can often be stated concisely.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 1 There is an infinite number of even numbers, impossible to list, but even numbers can be defined by saying that they are integer multiples of two.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: An extensional definition lists all the concepts corresponding to the objects in the extension. In defining classes, an extensional definition would list all the objects allowed within the intension of the class. This kind of definition is to be used only if the number of subordinate objects to be enumerated is limited, the list of subordinate objects is complete under one criterion of subdivision, and the subordinate objects are known.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXAMPLE 2 An extensional definition of the term "nation of the world" might be given by listing all of the nations of the world.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Extensional definitions are more frequently used to define concepts which correspond to properties. In many cases, a closed set of permissible values for a property can be presented as elements in the definition of the property. Such sets of permissible values may be the basis for consistency checking when users assign values to properties.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: # Annex F (informative)
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: # Conventions for writing definitions
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## F.1 General
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: In addition to the rules specified, Annex F provides additional guidance on the wording of definitions.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Below a high level overview is given of the conventions for writing definitions as laid down in the standards ISO/IEC 11179-4:2004 [5] and ISO 704:2009 (see Clause 2).
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## F.2.1 Requirements
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: A data definition shall:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: a) be stated in the singular;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: b) state what the concept is, not what it is not;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: c) be stated as one descriptive phrase or sentence;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: d) contain only commonly understood abbreviations;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: e) be expressed without embedding definitions of other data or underlying concepts.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## F.2.2 Recommendations
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: A data definition should:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: a) state the essential meaning of the concept;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: b) be precise and unambiguous;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: c) be concise;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: d) be able to stand alone;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: e) be expressed without embedding rationale, functional usage, or procedural information;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: f) avoid circular reasoning
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: g) use the same terminology and consistent logical structure for related definitions;
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: h) be appropriate for the type of metadata item being defined.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: The conventions set out in ISO 704 can be summarized as follows:
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: a) Define what it is, not what it is not.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: b) Define the concept, do not write a list of examples (extensional definitions, i.e., a list of subordinate concepts, are allowed in highly specialized domains only).
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: c) Avoid circular definitions.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: d) Do not define two concepts. A definition shall describe only one concept. It shall not include hidden definitions for any concepts used to identify characteristics. Any characteristic that requires an explanation shall be defined separately as a concept or given in a note.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: e) A definition is valid if it can replace a designation in a text without loss of or change in meaning.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: f) Definitions shall be as brief as possible and as complex as necessary. Complex definitions can contain several dependent clauses, but carefully written definitions contain only that information which makes the concept unique. Any additional descriptive information deemed necessary should be included in a note.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: g) The definition should not contain characteristics that belong logically to super ordinate or subordinate concepts.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: h) A definition shall describe the content of the concept precisely. It shall be neither too narrow nor too broad.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: ## F.4 Additional conventions
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: a) The term "value" shall not be written in plural even if it is a level type (e.g., minimum, typical and maximum value)
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: b) Always include the term "value" in the definition for quantitative DETs except for conditional data element types.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: c) Changing attributes to conform to the new conventions of this part of IEC 61360 is by default a revision change (minor change) unless specified otherwise, and will only be done along with a change request associated with the relevant data element type.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: 1) La Commission Electrotechnique Internationale (IEC) est une organisation mondiale de normalisation composée de l'ensemble des comités électrotechniques nationaux (Comités nationaux de l'IEC). L'IEC a pour objet de favoriser la coopération internationale pour toutes les questions de normalisation dans les domaines de l'électricité et de l'électronique. A cet effet, l'IEC – entre autres activités – publie des Normes internationales, des Spécifications techniques, des Rapports techniques, des Spécifications accessibles au public (PAS) et des Guides (ci-après dénommés "Publication(s) de l'IEC"). Leur élaboration est confiée à des comités d'études, aux travaux desquels tout Comité national intéressé par le sujet traité peut participer. Les organisations internationales, gouvernementales et non gouvernementales, en liaison avec l'IEC, participent également aux travaux. L'IEC collabore étroitement avec l'Organisation Internationale de Normalisation (ISO), selon des conditions fixées par accord entre les deux organisations.

layout_details.content: 2) Les décisions ou accords officiels de l'IEC concernant les questions techniques représentent, dans la mesure du possible, un accord international sur les sujets étudiés, étant donné que les Comités nationaux de l'IEC intéressés sont représentés dans chaque comité d'études.

layout_details.content: 3) Les Publications de l'IEC se présentent sous la forme de recommandations internationales et sont agréées comme telles par les Comités nationaux de l'IEC. layout_details.content: 4) Dans le but d'encourager l'uniformité internationale, les Comités nationaux de l'IEC s'engagent, dans toute la mesure possible, à appliquer de façon transparente les Publications de l'IEC dans leurs publications nationales et régionales. Toutes divergences entre toutes Publications de l'IEC et toutes publications nationales ou régionales correspondantes doivent être indiquées en termes clairs dans ces dernières.

layout_details.content: # INTRODUCTION
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: L'utilisation des données de produits constitue un élément essentiel du commerce électronique. Le choix des produits, les transactions commerciales, les procédures de maintenance, etc. reposent sur la disponibilité des données relatives aux produits et aux services. Afin d'assurer une compréhension commune et un traitement général des données de produits, des systèmes de classification et de dictionnaires sont utilisés pour définir leurs paramètres techniques essentiels ou pour catégoriser les produits.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Les normes de la série IEC 61360 établissent les règles de structure et de contenu des collections de propriétés de produits, ainsi que les structures de classification. Dans la plupart des cas, les classes et les propriétés figurant dans ces collections sont compréhensibles de manière intuitive. Mais, malheureusement, la création des objets d'information et de leur contenu textuel, par exemple les définitions, s'est avérée être une tâche astreignante comportant des pièges et des problèmes potentiels. Pour éviter ces difficultés, des documents explicatifs et des sections d'autres normes sont regroupés dans la présente partie de l'IEC 61360; ces éléments apportent les connaissances nécessaires à la création réussie de classes et de propriétés. C'est pourquoi l'IEC 61360-6 donne des lignes directrices pour la définition du contenu d'information des classes et propriétés de l'IEC 61360.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: La présente partie de l'IEC 61360 est destinée aux spécialistes du domaine, qui sont des experts techniques dans leur domaine technique spécifique. Les spécialistes du domaine ne doivent pas nécessairement avoir une connaissance approfondie des Normes IEC 61360-1 ou IEC 61360-2.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: EXEMPLE L'ensemble de produits utilisés par une entreprise particulière et l'ensemble de tous les produits normalisés ISO sont deux exemples de contextes. Dans ces deux contextes (l'entreprise particulière et l'ISO), l'ensemble des produits considérés comme membres de la classe des roulements à une rangée de billes peut être différent, en particulier parce que les employés de chaque entreprise ignorent l'existence d'un certain nombre de produits de type roulement à une rangée de billes.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Note 1 à l'article: Un produit conforme à la propriété abstraite définie par une classe est appelé membre de classe.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Note 2 à l'article: Une classe est un concept intentionnel qui peut revêtir différentes significations par extension dans différents contextes.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Note 3 à l'article: Les classes sont structurées par des relations d'inclusion de classes.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Note 4 à l'article: Une classe de produits est un concept général, tel qu'il est défini dans l'ISO 1087-1. Il est donc conseillé d'utiliser les règles définies dans l'ISO 704 pour définir les attributs de désignation et de définition des classes de produits.
layout_details.label: text

layout_details.content: Note 5 à l'article: Dans le contexte de la série ISO 13584, une classe est soit une classe de caractérisation, associée aux propriétés et utilisable pour caractériser les produits, soit une classe de catégorisation, qui n'est pas associée aux propriétés et qui n'est pas utilisable pour caractériser les produits.
layout_details.label: text

definition
